# Straighten a photo

- Route: `/tools/straighten-photo`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `photo`
- Slug: `straighten-photo`

## Summary

Fix a tilted horizon by angle or by drawing a line, then auto-crop to the largest rectangle. (Photo editing)

## Details

Straighten lives in the Geometry panel of Aperture and is applied to the source pixels before any adjustment layer. You can type an angle in degrees, or press Draw a line and drag along something that should be level or upright; the editor computes the tilt of your line, folds it into the range -45 to 45 degrees, and sets the rotation to cancel it. Rotation is one inverse-mapped bilinear resample, so pixels are sampled exactly once. By default the frame auto-crops to the largest centered rectangle, in the proportions of the rotated canvas, that contains only real pixels; turn that off and the corners are filled with transparency, the stretched edge, or a color you choose. The crop, flips and perspective share the same single resample.
### What it does
- Rotates by any angle from -360 to 360 degrees with a single bilinear resample of the original pixels; 90 and 180 degree steps are exact copies.
- Sets the angle from a line you draw: the tilt of the line is wrapped into (-45, 45] degrees and subtracted, so a line along a horizon or a door frame both work.
- Auto-crops to the largest centered rectangle in the proportions of the rotated canvas whose entire perimeter lands inside the rotated source, found by a 30-step binary search.
- Fills empty corners with transparency, the clamped edge pixel, or a solid color when you prefer to keep the whole rotated frame.
- Keeps masks aligned: every mask is stored in the straightened, cropped space, and the export renders the same geometry on the original.
### How to use it
1. Drop the photo: The Geometry panel opens in front with the Straighten section and the Draw a line button.
2. Draw along the horizon: Click Draw a line, drag from one end of the horizon to the other; a drag shorter than 8 px is ignored. The angle field updates.
3. Check the crop: Auto-crop to the largest rectangle is on by default. Turn it off and pick a fill if you want the corners kept.
4. Export: The server rotates and crops the original at full resolution and encodes JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF or TIFF.
### Supported formats
- Input: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF, BMP
- Output: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, TIFF
- A transparent corner fill survives only in PNG, WebP, AVIF and TIFF; JPG has no alpha and shows the fill as black.
- Daily limits and file caps depend on the plan; quote them only from the live plan block.
### Technical details
- The rotated canvas grows to the bounding box of the rotated source: width |w cos| + |h sin|, height |w sin| + |h cos|, rounded. A 6000 x 4000 photo rotated 2.5 degrees has a 6169 x 4258 canvas. Each output pixel center is mapped back through the crop, the perspective homography, the flips and the inverse rotation to a continuous source coordinate and sampled bilinearly from its four neighbors; coordinates outside the source take the fill.
- Auto-crop searches for the largest scale s of a centered rectangle in the aspect of the canvas such that all 100 sample points along its perimeter (25 per side) map inside the source, by binary search on s for 30 iterations. For 2.5 degrees on 6000 x 4000 that gives a crop of 88.44 percent of the canvas in each direction, 5456 x 3766 pixels (1.45:1, the canvas proportions), 20.55 MP, keeping 85.6 percent of the original pixels. At 1.2 degrees it keeps 92.5 percent, at 5 degrees about 75 percent.
- Draw a line: the angle of the line in screen coordinates (y down) is atan2(dy, dx) in degrees, reduced by multiples of 90 into (-45, 45], and its negative is added to the current rotation, rounded to 0.01 degree. A line from (200, 1080) to (1800, 1020) on a 1920 px preview is a 2.15 degree tilt and sets the rotation to +2.15.
- Fill: Transparent writes RGBA 0 outside the source (PNG and WebP keep it; JPG shows it as black), Stretch the edge clamps the sample to the nearest edge texel, and Color writes an opaque #rrggbb. Bilinear interpolation is also applied to the alpha channel, so a transparent fill has a one-pixel soft border.
- Aperture previews on your GPU (WebGL2) from a 1920 px copy, renders the export on our server from the original at full resolution with the same formulas, and the two agree within a small documented tolerance: for geometry that is a maximum of 2 8-bit levels over the interior with a 2 px border excluded, since the bilinear sample positions differ slightly at the two scales; color operations are held to a mean of 1 level and grain is exact.
### When not to use it
Do not use straighten when the lines in the photo converge rather than tilt: a building that leans back because the camera pointed upward needs the four-corner perspective tool, and rotating it only trades one tilted wall for another. For a plain 90 degree turn use the Rotate 90 degrees buttons, which copy pixels exactly with no resample. If you only need the EXIF orientation flag applied so the file displays the right way up, a resize or metadata tool handles that without opening an editor project.
### Use cases
- Seascapes and sunsets: Draw along the water line. A 1.5 degree correction on a 24 MP frame keeps 90.8 percent of the pixels.
- Buildings and doorways: Draw along a vertical edge instead; the angle wraps into the same -45 to 45 range so uprights work as well as horizons.
- Scanned documents and prints: Draw along the paper edge, use Stretch the edge as the fill, and export PNG so nothing is re-compressed.
- Phone photos taken in a hurry: A 2 degree fix on a 4032 x 3024 shot costs about 10 percent of the pixels and still leaves 11 MP.
### FAQ
Q: How much of the photo do I lose when straightening?
A: It depends on the angle and the aspect. On a 3:2 frame, 1 degree keeps about 94 percent of the pixels, 2.5 degrees about 86 percent and 5 degrees about 75 percent, with the auto-crop keeping the proportions of the rotated canvas.
Q: Can I keep the corners instead of cropping?
A: Yes. Switch off Auto-crop to the largest rectangle and choose a fill: Transparent for PNG or WebP output, Stretch the edge to smear the border pixels outward, or Color for a solid fill.
Q: Does rotating by a small angle blur the photo?
A: A single bilinear resample softens very slightly, about what a half-pixel shift does. The editor never resamples twice for straighten plus crop, and 90 and 180 degree turns are exact.
Q: Which way is positive rotation?
A: Positive angles rotate clockwise on screen. Drawing a line that slopes down to the right produces a positive correction that lifts the right side.
Q: Can I straighten a vertical line instead of the horizon?
A: Yes. Any line within 45 degrees of vertical is treated as something that should be upright, so a lamp post or door edge sets the same rotation a horizon would.
Q: What happens to a mask I painted before straightening?
A: Masks live in the corrected frame. Changing the crop re-maps every mask coordinate and re-samples brush strokes into the new space in the same edit, so the adjustment stays on the same picture content.
